say: Welcome back, inquirers! Today we are detectives again, and the clue is an angle. Surveyors, builders and pilots all use angles to find things they cannot measure. We will find angles without using a protractor at all.
Notice it, test it, explain why. Today "explain why" has a special meaning: every angle you find needs a REASON.
Here are four angles. You are not allowed a protractor. Use the corner of your paper: that is 90°. Fold it in half: that is 45°. Write your guesses on your whiteboard.
Which was the hardest to guess? How did you decide?
Draw any triangle and tear off the three corners. What do you think will happen when you put the corners together side by side? Write it down before you try.
Now a four-sided shape. Will the four corners fit on a straight line, or round a point?
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: put the three pointed corners together so that the points touch. Are they flat along the bottom?
Corners do not fit: draw a long straight line first and put the corners along it.
If a pair wants more: draw a triangle with a right angle. Do the corners still fit the same way?

say: “I want the angle next to 75° on a straight line. A straight line is 180°, so 180 take away 75 is 105. My reason: angles on a straight line add up to 180°.”
“Triangle with 50° and 30°: the three angles add up to 180°, so the third is 180 − 50 − 30 = 100°. My reason: angles in a triangle add up to 180°.”
“This triangle is isosceles and the top angle is 50°. The other two angles are equal. 180 − 50 = 130, and 130 ÷ 2 = 65 each. My reason: base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.”

do: Ask: “What is your reason for that angle?”
Ask: “Which angle did you find first? Which angle does it help you find next?”
Ask: “Do your angles add up to 180° in each triangle? Check.”
stuck: Hint 1: “Write down every angle you know first.”
Hint 2: “Look for a straight line, a triangle or a pair of equal sides. Each one gives you an angle fact.”
Hint 3: “Find ONE new angle and give its reason. Then look again: what can you find with it?”

do: Ask: “What is your reason for that angle?”
Ask: “Which angle did you find first? Which angle does it help you find next?”
Ask: “Do your angles add up to 180° in each triangle? Check.”
stuck: Hint 1: “Write down every angle you know first.”
Hint 2: “Look for a straight line, a triangle or a pair of equal sides. Each one gives you an angle fact.”
Hint 3: “Find ONE new angle and give its reason. Then look again: what can you find with it?”

say: “Ravi says an isosceles triangle can have an angle bigger than 90°. Mei says it cannot. Who is right?”
“Can an isosceles triangle have a right angle? What are the other two angles?”
ask: “Ravi says an isosceles triangle can have an angle bigger than 90°. Mei says it cannot. Who is right?”

Ravi is right. An isosceles triangle can have one big angle: for example 120°, 30°, 30°. It cannot have two angles of 90° or more, because they would already add up to 180° or more. It can have exactly one right angle: 90°, 45°, 45°. Mei is thinking of the base angles, and she is right about those: the two equal base angles are always less than 90°.

say: “Today you chased angles with reasons. A detective who can say why is much harder to argue with. Well done, inquirers!”
“Show me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p5l8-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Use the angle facts (straight line 180°, point 360°, vertically opposite, triangle 180°, isosceles and equilateral triangles, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium) to chase unknown angles through a figure, step by step, giving a reason for every step; list every case when only one angle of an isosceles triangle is given. Thinking strategies taught today: WRITE DOWN WHAT YOU KNOW, FIND ONE ANGLE AND SAY WHY, and TRY EVERY CASE. Drawings are not to scale: never measure. Materials: paper, ruler, pencil, scissors, protractor (only for the explore activity), red and blue pencils, mini whiteboards, workbook. Online: children tear or cut the corners of a paper triangle and quadrilateral on camera. The tutor screen-shares the slides and draws on the figures with the annotation tool. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6 (one check for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6 to 12 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 12 to 24.5 (pair work 6.5 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 24.5 to 36.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36.5 to 41, workbook page 1 41 to 54 (the questions without a star; after question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 54 to 57.5, short teaching before page 2 57.5 to 60.5, workbook page 2 60.5 to 68 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 68 to 71, talk time 71 to 76.5 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 76.5 to 81.5, reflection 81.5 to 84 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 84 to 85, and the buffer 85 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation."

p5l8-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE check for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three (face to face, you may glance at papers held low as you walk round; online, nothing is held up to the camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: 60° (30° + 60° = 90°).; Q2: 142°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, and 180° − 38° = 142°. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: children say the answers together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE check for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l8-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Guess the Angle. Children hold up a corner of paper (90°) and a folded corner (45°) to the screen to compare. They write four guesses on whiteboards. Click to reveal each true size. Answers: A = 120°, B = 30°, C = 150°, D = 90°. Ask: "Which was easiest? Why?" (90° is a square corner.) "Is C bigger or smaller than a straight line?" (smaller: a straight line is 180°.) Score: a guess within 10° is a point. Listen for children comparing with 90° and 45°: that is estimating with a benchmark, the same skill as in Lesson 1. Do not use the protractor yet.

p5l8-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 12. Read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click to show. Ask "What is your reason?" each time. 1) Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: 55°. 2) Angles at a point add up to 360°: 150 + 90 + 80 = 320, so 40°. 3) Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180 − 90 − 35 = 55°. 4) The two base angles are equal: (180 − 40) ÷ 2 = 70°. Answers: 55°, 40°, 55°, 70°. If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l8-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 24.5 (the whole explore; this slide 12 to 20.5). Children draw a triangle (any shape: one fat, one thin, one with a right angle is best), colour the corners and tear them off. They must predict first (thumbs: a straight line, a curve, a gap?). Then they fit the corners together with the points touching: the three corners make a straight line. Then the four-sided shape: the four corners fit round a point. Pair work is at most 6.5 minutes. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): a different triangle. Is it still a straight line? Online: children describe the torn corners aloud. Protractor optional: measure the three corners of one triangle and add them up (they will be close to 180°, not exact: that is the nature of measuring). PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6.5 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 20.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: 540°, which is one and a half turns (360° + 180°). A five-sided shape can be cut into 3 triangles from one corner, and 3 × 180° = 540°. A four-sided shape gives 2 triangles, 360°.

p5l8-explore2.note: Minutes 20.5 to 24.5. Pencils down: gather the pairs. Answers: 1) The three corners make a straight line, so the angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 2) The four corners fit round a point, so the angles of a four-sided shape add up to 360°. (Not asked together: does it work for every triangle? How could you find out?) Test very different triangles: a fat one, a thin one, a right-angled one. It works every time. Say: "This is a fact we can use to FIND angles without measuring." Extension: why is it 360°? Draw a line from one corner to the opposite corner: two triangles, 2 × 180° = 360°. Do not teach the method for the worksheet yet: the next slides do that. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): 540°, which is one and a half turns (360° + 180°). A five-sided shape can be cut into 3 triangles from one corner, and 3 × 180° = 540°. A four-sided shape gives 2 triangles, 360°.

p5l8-teach1.note: Minutes 24.5 to 26.5. Teach. These six facts are the reasons children will give all lesson. Read each card and ask children to say it back before you move on. 1) Straight line: 65° and 115° make 180°. 2) Point: 100 + 100 + 90 = 290, so the missing angle is 360 − 290 = 70°. 3) Vertically opposite: lines that cross make two pairs of equal angles (show it by folding paper or by turning a pair of sticks). 4) Triangle: 50 + 60 + 70 = 180 (like the corners we tore). 5) Isosceles: two equal sides, and the two angles at the bottom (the base angles) are equal. 36 + 72 + 72 = 180 is another example; here 72 + 54 + 54 = 180. 6) Equilateral: three equal sides and three 60° angles. Say: "A reason is one of these facts. Today every angle we find gets a reason."

p5l8-we1.note: Minutes 26.5 to 28.5. Click to reveal each step and its arc on the figure. Ask children to say the step before each click. Write the reason every time: that is the whole lesson. Think-aloud: "I know two angles in triangle PQS: 50 and 75. The three angles in a triangle add up to 180, so the third one, QPS, is 55. Reason: angles in a triangle." Step 2: "S is on the line QR, so angle PSQ and angle PSR sit on a straight line: 180 − 75 = 105." Step 3: "Now triangle PSR has 105 and 30, so SPR is 180 − 135 = 45." Step 4 is a check: the whole angle at P (QPR) is 55 + 45 = 100, so triangle PQR has 50 + 100 + 30 = 180. Ask: "Is the drawing to scale?" (No: never measure. We use facts.)

p5l8-try1.note: Minutes 28.5 to 30. Whiteboards: answer AND reason. a) 180° − 112° = 68° (straight line). b) 180° − 36° = 144°, 144° ÷ 2 = 72° (isosceles: base angles equal; triangle 180°). Ask: "Which reason did you give?" Accept any correct fact. (Two items only.)

p5l8-teachshapes.note: Minutes 30 to 32. Teach. Show each shape and ask: "What do you notice about the angles?" Parallelogram: opposite angles are equal (70° and 70°, 110° and 110°) and neighbouring angles add up to 180° (70 + 110). Rhombus: it is a parallelogram with all four sides equal, so the same angle facts, AND its equal sides make isosceles triangles when we draw a diagonal. Trapezium: only one pair of parallel sides (the arrows). Each slanted side joins the two parallel sides, and the two angles on it add up to 180°: 100 + 80 and 65 + 115. Check: 100 + 65 + 115 + 80 = 360, the angles in any four-sided shape. Click to show the last line.

p5l8-we2.note: Minutes 32 to 34. Click to reveal each step. Step 1: neighbouring angles of a rhombus (a parallelogram) add up to 180°. Step 2: ask first "Which sides are equal?" All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so AB = AD and triangle ABD is isosceles with apex A = 50°. The base angles are (180 − 50) ÷ 2 = 65° each. Step 3: angle ABC is 130° and ABD is 65°, so DBC = 65° too. Notice the diagonal cuts the angle into two equal parts: true for every rhombus. Think-aloud: "A diagonal turns a four-sided shape into triangles. Triangles are where my facts live." Check: triangle BCD is also isosceles (BC = CD): angle C = 50°, so 50 + 65 + 65 = 180 ✓.

p5l8-try2.note: Minutes 34 to 35.5. Whiteboards: angles AND reasons. a) 65° opposite, and 180° − 65° = 115° twice. b) D = 180° − 95° = 85°; C = 180° − 60° = 120° (angles between the parallel sides add up to 180°). Check: 95 + 60 + 120 + 85 = 360 ✓. (Two items only.)

p5l8-key.note: Minutes 35.5 to 36.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Measuring or guessing from the picture instead of using an angle fact: drawings are not to scale. (2) Calling the wrong angles equal in an isosceles triangle: the equal angles are the base angles, opposite the equal sides, not the angle between the equal sides. (3) Giving only one case when one angle of an isosceles triangle is known (the given angle could be the top angle or a base angle).

p5l8-break.note: Minutes 36.5 to 41. 4.5 minutes. Online: children make the angle with their arms on camera. Ask: "Show me 180° with ONE arm and the floor." Let a child be the caller. Call 270° (three quarters of a turn) as a surprise. Then a drink of water.

p5l8-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 54. Walk around. Ask "What is your reason?" before giving any help. Q2b: the hint says PQ = QR, so triangle PQR is isosceles with the 116° angle at the top. Remind children that the drawings are not to scale. Q2 (c) is take-home (starred); do not wait for it. Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 2 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 (a) to (d) and Q2 (a) (b). Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l8-ws1ans.note: Minutes 54 to 57.5. Click after a pair explains theirs, with the REASON. Q1a: 180° − 68° = 112° (straight line). Q1b: vertically opposite angle to AOC. Q1c: vertically opposite BOC. Q1d: angles at a point add up to 360°. Q2a: neighbouring angles add up to 180° (108°), opposite angles equal (72°, 108°). Q2b: neighbouring angles of the rhombus: 180° − 64° = 116°; triangle PQR has PQ = QR, so the base angles are equal: (180° − 116°) ÷ 2 = 32°. Q2c: angles between the parallel sides AB and DC add up to 180°: D = 180° − 110° = 70°, C = 180° − 80° = 100°. Check: 110 + 80 + 100 + 70 = 360.

p5l8-teachchain.note: Minutes 57.5 to 59. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 is a chain with an isosceles triangle; this one has different angles and the equal sides are different). Ask first: "Which two sides are equal? So which two angles are equal?" DA = DC, so the equal angles are the ones opposite them: angle C and angle DAC. Click 1: DAC = 35°. Click 2: triangle ADC: 180 − 35 − 35 = 110°. Click 3: B, D, C are on a straight line, so ADB + ADC = 180°: 70°. Click 4: triangle ABD has 45° and 70°, so ABD = 65°. Check: triangle ABC has B = 65, C = 35 and angle BAC = 45 + 35 = 80: 65 + 35 + 80 = 180 ✓. Say: "A chain: each angle helps me find the next, and each has a reason."

p5l8-teachcombo.note: Minutes 59 to 60.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 is a parallelogram with an isosceles triangle, two steps; the shape here is different. Think harder A3 continues the figure of Q4). Ask first: "Which two sides are equal, XY and XZ. Which angles are opposite them?" Angle XZY (opposite XY) and angle XYZ (opposite XZ): both 55°. Click 1: 55°. Click 2: triangle XYZ: 180 − 110 = 70°. Click 3: in the parallelogram neighbouring angles add up to 180°, so angle WXY = 180 − 55 = 125°. Click 4: angle WXY is made of two smaller angles, WXZ and ZXY, so WXZ = 125 − 70 = 55°. Check: triangle WXZ: angle W is 55° (opposite angle to Y), and 55 + 55 = 110, so angle WZX = 70°, which with XZY = 55° makes angle Z = 125° ✓ (neighbouring angles Y and Z add up to 180°).

p5l8-ws2.note: Minutes 60.5 to 68. Children work alone. The strip of reasons A to F is printed at the top of page 2: children write a letter (or words) for Q3(b) and (d); the first step of Q3 is worked for them. Q3 (c) (d) and Q5 are take-home (starred). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who measure. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q3 (b) and Q4 (a) (b), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 68 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l8-ws2ans.note: Minutes 68 to 71. One child explains Q3 (b) with the reason; click through the rest (Q3 (c) (d) and Q5 are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click after a child explains WITH reasons. Q3: AB = AD, so the base angles ADB and B are equal: 62°. BAD = 180° − 62° − 62° = 56°. ADC = 180° − 62° = 118° (straight line). ACD = 180° − 118° − 38° = 24°. Check: angle BAC = 56° + 38° = 94° and 62° + 94° + 24° = 180° ✓. Q4: ADC = ABC = 56° (opposite angles). DA = DE: DEA = (180° − 56°) ÷ 2 = 62°. AEC = 180° − 62° = 118° (straight line). Angle DAB = 180° − 56° = 124°; DAE = 62°, so EAB = 124° − 62° = 62°. Q5a: 50° as a base angle gives 50°, 50°, 80°; 50° as the top angle gives 65°, 65°. Q5b: 100° cannot be a base angle (two of them make 200°), so only 100°, 40°, 40°.

p5l8-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) A = 135° and B = 45°. Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180°, so A and B make 4 equal parts of 45°: B = 45°, A = 135°. A2) 35° and 35°. 110° cannot be a base angle (two of them would be 220°), so it is the top angle and 180° − 110° = 70° is shared by two equal base angles. A3) AEC = 118° and EAB = 62°. ADC = 56° (opposite angles); DEA = (180° − 56°) ÷ 2 = 62° (DA = DE); AEC = 180° − 62° = 118° (straight line DC); DAB = 180° − 56° = 124° (neighbours in a parallelogram), so EAB = 124° − 62° = 62°. A4) ADE = 150° (90° + 60°). Triangle ADE is isosceles (AD = DE), so DAE = (180° − 150°) ÷ 2 = 15°.

p5l8-stretch2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) A = 135° and B = 45°. Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180°, so A and B make 4 equal parts of 45°: B = 45°, A = 135°. A2) 35° and 35°. 110° cannot be a base angle (two of them would be 220°), so it is the top angle and 180° − 110° = 70° is shared by two equal base angles. A3) AEC = 118° and EAB = 62°. ADC = 56° (opposite angles); DEA = (180° − 56°) ÷ 2 = 62° (DA = DE); AEC = 180° − 62° = 118° (straight line DC); DAB = 180° − 56° = 124° (neighbours in a parallelogram), so EAB = 124° − 62° = 62°. A4) ADE = 150° (90° + 60°). Triangle ADE is isosceles (AD = DE), so DAE = (180° − 150°) ÷ 2 = 15°.

p5l8-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 30°. Angles B and C are (180° − 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°. In triangle BCD, BD = BC, so angle BDC = angle C = 70°, which makes angle CBD = 40°. Then ABD = 70° − 40° = 30°. B2) 150°. AE = AB = AD, so triangle ADE is isosceles with angle DAE = 90° − 60° = 30°, which makes angle AED = 75°. In the same way angle BEC = 75°. Angle AEB = 60°. Round E: 360° − 75° − 75° − 60° = 150°. B3) Two sets: 50°, 50°, 80° and 40°, 70°, 70°. (If the top angle is 30° bigger than a base angle: 3 equal parts and 30° make 180°, so base 50°. If a base angle is 30° bigger than the top: top 40°, base 70°.) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Draw a triangle and a parallelogram that share a side. Give two or three angles and ask for one more. Swap and solve. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l8-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) 30°. Angles B and C are (180° − 40°) ÷ 2 = 70°. In triangle BCD, BD = BC, so angle BDC = angle C = 70°, which makes angle CBD = 40°. Then ABD = 70° − 40° = 30°. B2) 150°. AE = AB = AD, so triangle ADE is isosceles with angle DAE = 90° − 60° = 30°, which makes angle AED = 75°. In the same way angle BEC = 75°. Angle AEB = 60°. Round E: 360° − 75° − 75° − 60° = 150°. B3) Two sets: 50°, 50°, 80° and 40°, 70°, 70°. (If the top angle is 30° bigger than a base angle: 3 equal parts and 30° make 180°, so base 50°. If a base angle is 30° bigger than the top: top 40°, base 70°.) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Draw a triangle and a parallelogram that share a side. Give two or three angles and ask for one more. Swap and solve. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l8-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. The tick marks show equal sides. Ask: What do you notice? Which triangles are isosceles? Which angles must be equal? In B2, how long is AE compared with AD? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l8-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. B1: the tick marks tell us which triangles are isosceles. Triangle ABC: AB = AC with top angle 40°, so B = C = 70°. Triangle BCD: BD = BC, so the angles opposite them are equal: angle BDC = angle BCD = 70°. Then angle CBD = 180° − 140° = 40°. Angle ABD = angle ABC − CBD = 70° − 40° = 30°. Q2: AB = AE (equilateral) and AB = AD (square), so AE = AD and triangle ADE is isosceles. Angle DAE = angle DAB − angle EAB = 90° − 60° = 30°, so each base angle is 75°. The same happens on the right: BEC = 75°. The four angles round E add up to 360°: DEA 75° + AEB 60° + BEC 75° + the angle DEC: 360° − 210° = 150°.

p5l8-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 76.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: Ravi is right. An isosceles triangle can have one big angle: for example 120°, 30°, 30°. It can also have one right angle: 90°, 45°, 45°. It cannot have two angles of 90° or more, because they would already add up to 180° or more. The two equal BASE angles are always less than 90°, so Mei is right about those. Second question if time: "How do you know you have found every case?" (we tried the given angle as the top angle and as a base angle). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l8-exit.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. Answer: 68°. Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180° − 44° = 136°. PQ = PR, so the base angles are equal: 136° ÷ 2 = 68°. Accept any clear reasons. Extension: draw a triangle and put the three angle labels 40°, 60° and 80° on the corners. Cut the corners off and fit them together. Now do the same with any four-sided shape. Explain in one sentence why a four-sided shape always gives 360°. (Draw a line from one corner to the opposite corner: two triangles, 2 × 180° = 360°.)

p5l8-reflect.note: Minutes 81.5 to 84. REFLECTION, about a minute and a half.
